name: Atlas
license: Open core: Community Edition is Apache 2.0; the standard binary adds proprietary features under the Atlas MSA, some of them paid (Atlas Pro)
summary: A schema-as-code tool, “Terraform for databases”: you describe the schema you want in SQL, HCL or ORM models, and Atlas plans, lints, tests and applies the migrations to get there.
intro: Atlas manages a database schema the way Terraform manages infrastructure. You write the desired schema as SQL, as Atlas HCL, or let Atlas read it from your ORM: it has loaders for 16 ORMs in six languages, including GORM and Ent in Go, Prisma, Drizzle and TypeORM in TypeScript, Django and SQLAlchemy in Python, Hibernate, EF Core and Doctrine. Atlas then inspects the target database, computes the difference, and plans the DDL. To understand the schema exactly as the database would, it applies it to a throwaway “dev database”, often a container started from a URL such as `docker://postgres/16/dev`.

It supports two workflows. In the declarative one, `atlas schema apply` moves a database straight to the desired state, like `terraform apply`. In the versioned one, `atlas migrate diff` writes the next migration file into a folder, and `atlas migrate apply` runs the files not yet applied. Either way, more than 50 analyzers lint the plan for dropped tables or columns, changes that fail on existing data such as a `NOT NULL` column without a default, and locks or table rewrites that would block a busy table. It also tests functions, views and triggers from `.test.hcl` files, and manages roles, permissions and row-level security policies as code.

Atlas is written in Go. It supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server, ClickHouse, Redshift, Oracle, Snowflake, CockroachDB, TiDB, Databricks, Spanner, Aurora DSQL and Azure Fabric, and runs from the CLI, GitHub Actions and other CI systems, a Kubernetes operator, a Terraform provider or a Go SDK. The free Starter tier covers MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQLite with basic features; Pro starts at $9 per developer a month, plus $59 a month per CI/CD project and $39 per monitored database, and adds all databases, linting in CI, drift detection, schema monitoring and audit trails in Atlas Cloud. The latest release is 1.3.0 (August 2, 2026).
strengths: Plans migrations for you from the desired schema, in either a declarative or a versioned workflow
Migration linting that knows each database: destructive changes, data-dependent changes, locks and rewrites
Reads schemas from many ORMs, so teams keep using their models as the source of truth
Fits infrastructure pipelines: Terraform provider, Kubernetes operator, CI actions and IAM authentication to RDS and Cloud SQL
limits: Open core: the Apache 2.0 Community Edition lacks linting, testing, views, triggers, functions and drivers such as SQL Server, ClickHouse and Oracle, which are in the free-to-download but proprietary standard binary
Many features need `atlas login` and a paid Pro plan, priced per developer, per pipeline and per monitored database
Planning needs a dev database of the same engine, usually a Docker container, available wherever Atlas runs
An automatically planned migration still needs review: a rename can look like a drop and an add, and lint catches only what its analyzers know

story: Ariel Mashraki joined Facebook’s Connectivity team in Tel Aviv in 2018 and wrote Ent, a graph-based ORM for Go, which Facebook open-sourced in October 2019 and which later moved to the Linux Foundation. The creators of Ent went on to found Ariga, with Mashraki as CEO and Rotem Tamir as co-founder, to build database tooling. On November 25, 2021 Ariga open-sourced the Atlas CLI, describing schemas in HCL, “similar to Terraform”, and arguing that managing database schemas needed the kind of machine-readable definitions that Chef, Puppet and Terraform had brought to infrastructure.

On June 1, 2023 Ariga announced it had raised $18 million from Tiger Global and TLV Partners. Atlas grew from a declarative tool into one that also plans versioned migration files, reads ORM models, lints, tests and monitors schemas, and added commercial databases such as Oracle, Snowflake and Databricks. The project follows an open-core model: the Apache 2.0 Community Edition is built from the public repository, while the standard binary adds proprietary features. Atlas 1.0 came out on December 23, 2025, which its team said reflected a tool that had been production-ready for years.

choices.choice: Desired state instead of hand-written steps
choices.why: Writing migration files by hand is slow and error-prone. Describing the target and letting the tool compute the difference is how Terraform made infrastructure changes reviewable, and Ariga applied the same idea to schemas.

choices.choice: Normalize through a real dev database
choices.why: Databases store a schema in a canonical form that differs from how people write it, and parsing alone can’t tell whether every expression is valid. Running the desired schema through a scratch instance of the same engine validates it and lets Atlas compare normalized forms, so it doesn’t propose needless changes.

choices.choice: Lint every migration before it runs
choices.why: A migration that drops a column or locks a large table can take an application down. Static checks in CI catch those changes during code review, the way a linter does for code.
The core engine stays Apache 2.0 so anyone can use and embed it, while features for teams, more databases and the cloud service pay for development.
